selectionSummary: Consistent selection: weigh international consequences, civilian and institutional stakes, breadth of independent coverage and possible lasting impact. Three separate events across Europe, the Middle East and Oceania were selected; their relative impact is an editorial judgment.

snapshot.summary: Ukraine's energy and transport links were hit ahead of peace talks; Israel's president made the first nomination in a deadlocked coalition contest; and New Zealand's vote offered no settled governing majority.
connections: Each story turns on resilience and control of essential systems: electricity and infrastructure, parliamentary coalitions and election procedures.
International diplomacy could be shaped by Ukraine's wartime pressure, Israel's future government and New Zealand's Pacific policy direction, but those downstream effects were not settled.
uncertainties: Kyiv's final repair timetable and next week's diplomatic consequences were unknown.
Israel's nominee had not yet built or formally received his governing mandate.
New Zealand's final ballots and coalition agreements remained outstanding.

stories.title: Russian attacks disrupt Kyiv energy links and damage its Northern Bridge
stories.summary: Russian strikes on November 6–7 damaged power infrastructure linked to Kyiv and the Northern Bridge; officials reported heating, power and water disruption. Ukrainian authorities described a large ballistic missile and drone attack. Russia characterized its targets as supporting Ukrainian military capabilities. A new round of US-brokered negotiations was scheduled for the following week.
stories.whyItMatters: Attacks on a European capital's grid and transport links threaten civilian survival during colder weather and could complicate negotiations in an ongoing cross-border war.
stories.selectionRationale: Severe attack on a major city's critical infrastructure with humanitarian, energy-security and negotiation implications; reported by independent international and domestic newsrooms.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters and Guardian report the effects; Interfax independently reports Russia's official target justification, which is attributed rather than verified. No historical captures.

stories.title: Herzog chooses Eisenkot for Israel's first post-election government-forming attempt
stories.summary: President Isaac Herzog announced November 7 that he would formally give Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government on Sunday. Parties representing 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot and 46 Netanyahu, but neither electoral bloc held a 61-seat majority. Arab-led parties' recommendations mattered despite disagreements about partnership.
stories.whyItMatters: The nomination could reshape Israeli leadership and regional diplomacy, but does not itself create a government or transfer power from caretaker Prime Minister Netanyahu.
stories.selectionRationale: Potential leadership change in a state with extensive international security and regional diplomacy implications; first substantial formal step after a deadlocked election.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters, Al Jazeera and an original Times of Israel Saturday liveblog update were opened; the Saturday announcement must not be conflated with the planned Sunday formal mandate.

commonFacts.text: Herzog announced on November 7 that he had selected Eisenkot to try to form the next government, with the formal ceremony set for November 8.
Eisenkot received the backing of parties representing 67 lawmakers compared with 46 for Netanyahu.
Neither the Eisenkot nor Netanyahu electoral bloc alone had 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament.
The government-forming candidate would have 28 days to secure a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

framingDifferences.text: Al Jazeera puts Arab-led lawmakers' electoral gains and possible coalition leverage at the center; The Times of Israel emphasizes legal procedure and party recommendations.
Reuters explores alternatives such as minority or unity government, while Al Jazeera reports Arab-party arguments for ending Netanyahu's government.
The Times of Israel carefully distinguishes the November 7 choice from a November 8 formal handover; some wider headlines use shorthand that could imply the mandate had already been delivered.

uncertainties: The formal mandate had not been handed over at the November 7 cutoff.
It was unknown whether Eisenkot could form a majority with any of the available blocs or external support.
Coalition negotiations could fail, potentially triggering further attempts or an election.

unverifiedClaims.reason: Reported intention, not proof that a viable agreement existed.

stories.title: New Zealand's tight election leaves government formation uncertain
stories.summary: Election-night returns on November 7 provisionally put the National-ACT-New Zealand First bloc on 67 seats, a razor-thin lead that could shift once special votes were counted. Neither Prime Minister Christopher Luxon nor Labour leader Chris Hipkins claimed a decisive victory. The new Opportunity Party was projected to enter parliament and might influence negotiations.
stories.whyItMatters: The result shapes Pacific diplomatic, trade, climate and domestic economic policy in a regional democracy, with small parties potentially deciding the government.
stories.selectionRationale: Major national election with exceptionally thin provisional governing margin, fragmented party support and prolonged uncertainty about regional policy direction.
stories.evidenceNote: Three originating newsrooms: Reuters, The Guardian and AP. Guardian revised its report after cutoff; only election-night points corroborated in independent contemporaneous reporting are used. AP first-publication clock not available.

commonFacts.text: Election-night calculations tentatively put the incumbent National-led grouping on approximately 67 parliamentary seats without a reliable final majority.
Special votes had not all been counted, and official results were expected on November 27.
Both National and Labour had party-vote support below roughly 30%, increasing smaller parties' importance.
The Opportunity Party was projected to enter parliament with seven seats, potentially altering coalition options.

framingDifferences.text: Reuters stresses caretaker arrangements, economic dissatisfaction and the coalition timetable, while The Guardian explains proportional voting and special-vote shifts.
AP foregrounds the new Opportunity Party and its leader Qiulae Wong, whereas Reuters focuses on the competing major-party leaders and coalition arithmetic.
Newsrooms projected parliament sizes near 130 or 131 as returns evolved, making a one-seat discrepancy in the majority threshold provisional, not a settled contradiction.

uncertainties: Final number of seats, size of parliament and governing margin could change with hundreds of thousands of special votes.
No definitive coalition agreement existed by cutoff.
Opportunity's eventual leverage and timing of coalition negotiations were unsettled.

unverifiedClaims.reason: Political forecast based on provisional numbers, not certified election results or a signed agreement.
